rationale: Interpreted the user-restore receipt and closed the repair question's second mechanism. Receipt 6ff0ef691a0141449142bfa06719bb47 evaluated all five comparisons: the leader's Restore call succeeded after its FSM caught up (holds, index 5), the restarted node's applied writes became the snapshot's majority write (holds, index 5), its minority write is gone (holds, index 5), and all five nodes' applied write lists agree afterwards (holds, index 5), with the feature-off control equally consistent (holds, index 12). That is the cluster-wide convergence the per-node installSnapshot path did not achieve, so the repair question now has both mechanisms with their scopes, the child and parent limitation lists are corrected accordingly, and the follower-side snapshot knowledge entry gained this receipt as an execution.

knowledge.statement: On a follower that receives an InstallSnapshot, the handler streams and finalises the snapshot, restores the FSM through fsmMutateCh, sets lastApplied and the last snapshot to the request's last log index and term, and replaces the latest and committed configuration from the request; the local log is then either removed entirely (monotonic stores) or compacted up to the snapshot index. A follower that has fallen behind a leader whose log was compacted is therefore sent a snapshot and ends up with the leader's FSM state, entry suffix and configuration, replacing any divergent entry it held at an index the leader also used.
knowledge.conditions: Triggered either because the leader can no longer serve the entries the follower needs (its log was compacted past the follower's position) or because the leader consumed a snapshot through the Restore contract and pushed it to its followers; observed with in-memory stores in both cases.

interpretations.rationale: The declared predicates about the public restore path are all satisfied. Admissions index 0 and index 6 record the shared structural fixture in both modes. In the feature-on run (index 5), after a current-configuration leader waited on a Barrier, took a snapshot and consumed it through Restore(meta, reader, 5s), the call returned without error, the restarted node's applied write list became majority-write, the minority write is absent, and the applied write lists of all five nodes agree, which the per-node installSnapshot receipt did not achieve. The feature-off control (index 12) is equally consistent. Mechanism: the leader takes on the snapshot state and its followers are sent an InstallSnapshot, whose handler restores the FSM, replaces the configuration and drops or compacts the local log (raft.go 1935-1972), so the divergent entry and the stale view are replaced cluster-wide through the paths the earlier receipts documented. Limits: the snapshot consumed is one the leader produced itself in the same run rather than an external backup, the harness had to wait for the FSM to catch up before snapshotting, one restored sample per mode was taken with in-memory stores, and the term-changing truncation path remains unexercised.
limitations: The restored snapshot was produced by the leader in the same run rather than supplied as an external backup file, and no index offset is applied.
One restored sample per mode; in-memory stores and scaled timeouts.
The term-changing truncation path is not exercised.
counterevidence: The control run reaching the same consistency shows the convergence is not specific to the defect run.
The earlier per-node repair receipt still shows that without a restore or a lagging follower the divergence persists, so this path is a further repair mechanism rather than the ordinary one.

interpretations.joint_history: Three receipts of three fixed experiments over the same divergent state: fa1f90c2eefd45e6af45d7593ac53205 records the healed state in which the entry and applied state differ across nodes; 112186e8b9544b51b4f7818a04c78a84 adds the repair phase in which a lagging restarted node installs a snapshot; 6ff0ef691a0141449142bfa06719bb47 further revises that harness to have the leader consume a snapshot through the Restore contract, which pushes it to the followers. They are compatible because all three observe the same cluster identity, conflict index and applied-write payloads (minority-write against majority-write), and the later receipt's fixture and healed events carry the same values as the earlier ones; each comparison outcome is read from its own receipt.
interpretations.rationale: Answer: two permitted mechanisms reconcile the divergent state, with different scopes, and one remains untested. A node that falls behind a compacted leader is sent a snapshot and ends up with the leader's FSM state, entry suffix and configuration (receipt 112186e8b9544b51b4f7818a04c78a84), but only that node is repaired. A leader-side restore converges the whole cluster: receipt 6ff0ef691a0141449142bfa06719bb47 shows the public Restore call succeeding on the leader and every node's applied write list agreeing afterwards, with the minority write gone from the restarted node. Both work through the InstallSnapshot handler (raft.go 1935-1972). What was not exercised is a truncation caused by a different term: an entry at the divergent index whose term differs would be overwritten through ordinary AppendEntries, which neither receipt covers. Remaining limits: the harness arranged the lag for the per-node repair and produced the restored snapshot itself; the samples are single per mode; in-memory stores with scaled timeouts were used.
limitations: Truncation of the divergent entry by a different term is not exercised.
The per-node repair needed harness-arranged lag and the cluster-wide repair used a snapshot the leader produced itself.
Single samples per mode with in-memory stores and scaled timeouts.
counterevidence: Without either mechanism the earlier receipts show the divergence persisting through a long run and a configuration change, so neither path is engaged by ordinary operation while the node keeps up.
The per-node repair leaves an up-to-date divergent node untouched, whereas the restore converges the cluster, so the two mechanisms are not interchangeable.

interpretations.joint_history: Eight receipts of seven fixed experiments over one defect chain, sharing the structural fixture (snapshot configuration {A,B,C}, a committed configuration entry with {A,B,C,D,E} above it, a persisted commit index covering it) and the feature-on restart reporting {A,B,C}, with the control run reporting {A,B,C,D,E}. They successively construct the restart state, observe the split, add healing, applied-state sampling, the per-node repair phase, the feature-off control, a long run and a configuration change, and finally the leader-side restore. Each comparison outcome is read from its own receipt, and later revisions restricted their comparison sets to new predicates.
interpretations.rationale: Answer, now with both repair mechanisms bounded: yes. A node left with a stale configuration by the RestoreCommittedLogs replay wins an election with fewer votes than the configuration recorded in its own committed log while the other voters elect their own leader, both sides commit at the same index and term, and after healing the entry and applied divergence survives a long run and a configuration change, while the stale membership itself ends at the next configuration change (receipt 182740a6d29f4af9a99cf83c49f2e857 index 4). The divergence is reconciled in two ways: an installed snapshot for a node that falls behind a compacted leader (receipt 112186e8b9544b51b4f7818a04c78a84), and a leader-side Restore that converges the whole cluster (receipt 6ff0ef691a0141449142bfa06719bb47 index 5, where every node's applied writes agree and the minority write is gone). Remaining limits: truncation of the divergent entry by a different term is unexercised; the per-node repair needed harness-arranged lag and the restore used a self-produced snapshot; the configuration change was a single harness-issued AddVoter; the long run is entry-count based; and in-memory stores with scaled timeouts and a graceful restart were used throughout.
limitations: Truncation of the divergent entry by a different term is not exercised.
The per-node repair needed harness-arranged lag and the cluster-wide repair used a snapshot the leader produced itself.
The configuration change is a single harness-issued AddVoter and the long run is ~200 entries without a snapshot install.
In-memory stores, scaled timeouts and a graceful shutdown rather than a crash.
counterevidence: The feature-off control run over the identical scenario, long run, configuration change and restore shows no stale membership, no minority leader and no self-applied write.
A later configuration entry ends the stale membership, and both repair paths remove the divergent entry and applied state, so neither consequence is permanent.
Without a repair the earlier receipts show the divergence persisting while the node keeps up, so the consequences are bounded by the repair timing rather than by ordinary operation.
